# C4 — Inefficient Control Flow

*Level 1 card. 8 root causes. Open the level-2 card before accepting any of them.*

Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization. This includes ordering conditions so expensive checks run before cheap ones (poor short-circuit ordering), evaluating conditions that are always true/false (redundant evaluation), using deeply nested branches instead of guard clauses (inefficient nesting), missing mutually-exclusive elif chains (missing else-if), using expensive type introspection in tight loops (expensive comparison), using try/except for frequent exception paths (expensive exception flow), not guarding against trivial edge cases (missing guards), and using non-Pythonic conditional idioms (non-idiomatic condition).

## Root causes in this category

| ID | Name | The repair | Measurable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | put the cheap, most-decisive test first so short-circuiting can skip the rest | yes, scales with input |
| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | delete the condition whose result is already known | **no — advisory only** |
| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | flatten with guard clauses that return early | **no — advisory only** |
| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | chain the branches with `elif` so evaluation stops at the first match | yes, scales with input |
| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | hoist the type decision out of the loop, or dispatch polymorphically | yes, scales with input |
| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | replace the frequently-raised exception with an explicit check | yes, scales with input |
| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | add a guard that returns immediately for the trivial case | yes, scales with call count |
| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | use the idiomatic form | yes, scales with input |

## If nothing here fits

Say so and move on. Reporting a weak match from an already-open category is the most common way this analysis goes wrong: the category is open because a static signal pointed at it, not because a smell is there.
